protocol_and_eligibility.review_title: Spinal manipulative therapy for adults with chronic low back pain
protocol_and_eligibility.research_question: What does this review evaluate: the benefits and harms of SMT compared to (1) sham SMT/placebo intervention, (2) no treatment, and (3) other conservative interventions in people with chronic LBP (18+ years old)?
protocol_and_eligibility.eligibility_inclusion_criteria:
- Study designs: We included only RCTs published as full texts. Cross-over and cluster-randomised trials were considered.
- Participants: Participants •Adults (≥ 18 years of age) •With a median duration of the current episode of LBP greater than 12 weeks for the study population, meaning that more than 50% of the study population had pain lasting longer than three months Studies •In which the unique contribution of SMT to the observed effects could be implied; that is, studies in which the effects of SMT could be isolated. This included studies in which SMT was delivered as part of a package of care; for example, studies comparing SMT plus exercise with exercise alone would be included, whereas studies comparing SMT plus exercise with SMT alone would not. •Studies with a mixed population, including participants with and witho.
- Interventions: Experimental intervention This review focusses on the effects of both spinal manipul.
protocol_and_eligibility.eligibility_exclusion_criteria:
- We excluded trials using an inadequate randomisation procedure (e.g. alternate allocation, allocation based upon birthdate).
- Participants •Postpartum LBP or pelvic pain due to pregnancy •Pain unrelated to the low back, e.g. coccydynia •Postoperative studies or participants with 'failed-back syndrome' •Serious pathologies, such as tumour, fracture, or infection Studies •Examined 'maintenance care' or prevention •Were designed to test the immediate post-intervention effect of a single treatment only, with no additional follow-up •Exclusively examined.

Blinding (performance bias and detection bias): All outcomes - patients: They were unaware of their group allocations and were informed only about the existence of two groups and not about the study’s objectives.
